issues.problem: 'Thursday, Friday, school with you!' says Friday is a school day. In most Gulf countries (Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman) Friday is the weekend and the main family/prayer day, so this line is wrong for many of the children.
'Saturday, Sunday, we play, play, play!' presents Saturday-Sunday as the weekend; in much of the Gulf Sunday is a school day. Keep the days neutral.
'Seven days in a week, and Tom is happy!' is not a natural sentence (no verb in the first part).
issues.suggestion: There are seven days in a week. Tom is happy!

issues.problem: 'Tom has a capital letter. Lucy has a capital letter.' sounds like the children Tom and Lucy are holding a letter; a 6-year-old will not understand that it is about their names.
issues.suggestion: Tom and Lucy are names. Names have capital letters.

issues.problem: After 'Tom, Anna, Sam and I,' the line 'A name has a capital letter' suggests that I is a name. The focus is names AND I.
issues.suggestion: Names and I have capital letters, my friend!

issues.problem: 'Show me a big letter.' - a child at a screen has nothing to show. Use the letter card and the lesson term.
'Say your name.' does not practise capitals or full stops.
issues.suggestion: Write your name with a capital letter.

issues.problem: 'Say Tom.' does not practise the focus (capital letters can only be seen in writing).
'Clap at the end of the sentence.' - there is no sentence being said at that moment, so the child cannot do it.
With the speaking commands replaced by writing ones, the lesson no longer practises naming people/things (PREA1-08).
'Point to the cup.' - there is no cup card (cards: milk, water, juice, rice, chicken, bread), so there is nothing to point to.
'Show me a spoon.' - a child at a screen or desk usually has no spoon, and there is no spoon card.
'Five, fifteen, fifty!' is a list, not part of the story; the narrator suddenly counts and 'five' has no meaning in the story.
issues.suggestion: Grace paints for fifty minutes. She paints five flowers.

issues.problem: The kite is in a tree, then 'Now Nick is happy' with no reason; a young child cannot follow the jump. Give the small happy end.
issues.suggestion: Dad gets the kite. Nick is happy. We are happy!

issues.problem: 'Say he is seven.' contradicts the story: Eva (she) is seven and Nick (he) is ten.
'Point to your friend.' - the child is alone at the screen and there is no friend card.
